title: Can I use artificial intelligence to prepare a Bible study?
description: A support tool that still requires personal reading, verification, and responsibility in teaching.
answer: You can use artificial intelligence as a support for organizing questions or exploring an explanation, as long as you check the content. The responsibility to read the passage, evaluate the sources, and teach faithfully is still yours. A fluent answer can contain invented quotations or interpretations the text does not support.
sections: Begin with the passage you are going to study

Second Timothy 2:15 calls us to handle the word of truth accurately. The task of teaching requires attention to the text. Before asking for an automatic explanation, read the whole passage and notice who is speaking, who is being addressed, and how it relates to what comes before.

Write down your questions and consult a reliable translation. A tool can help you organize your observations, but it cannot take on for you the willingness to listen. It is important to distinguish what you see in the passage from an idea that appeared in a generated answer.

Acts 17:10–12 describes people who examined the Scriptures to evaluate what they heard. The episode invites us to receive teaching attentively and to test it. If an answer mentions a verse, a historical fact, or a Greek word, check that the reference exists and supports the claim.

Ask for identifiable sources and open them. The tool can combine true information with incorrect information, and it can also present one particular interpretation as if it were the only one. Compare explanations and recognize when a question remains open or requires more study.
Keeping the responsibility of the one who teaches

James 3:1 warns about the responsibility of teachers. Copying material without reviewing it does not transfer that responsibility to the system that produced it. If you cannot explain a claim or show where it comes from, avoid teaching it as a settled conclusion.

You must also take care with words attributed to other people. Do not present generated text as a quotation from an author or as your own experience. If the tool played a significant part in the material, describe how you used it honestly, in keeping with the setting of your community.
Using the help wisely and caring for people

First Thessalonians 5:21 points us to testing and recognizing what is good. You can make use of a suggested outline, a list of questions, or clearer wording, after evaluating them. Speed must not become the main criterion for preparing a lesson.

Avoid entering other people’s confidences or private information into a tool without their permission. To walk alongside someone, you need listening, prayer, and a responsible relationship. Preparation can receive technical support; pastoral care and accountability require people who are present.
